prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reached a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B029, Katori and Ye. Round 1 did not weaken it; it sharpened what the citation has to say. The achievement is the lattice clock itself, meaning the magic-wavelength trap that cancels the light shift while holding many atoms free of Doppler and recoil effects, and its realisation at the 10^-18 level. The chair's first question was whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes leave this as a separate step. I think they do. The 2005 prize honoured the comb and laser spectroscopy, which is how the clock is read out. The 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. Neither solved the problem of getting a large atom number and freedom from motional shifts at the same time, and that is what Katori's scheme does. Ye's group then showed that this design reaches the 10^-18 regime and exposes relativistic and many-body effects inside the clock. The result is reproduced and intercompared at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, which is the experimental standard I weigh most. On the second question, I want the citation to rest only on what has been demonstrated: the invention and the achieved precision. I would not put the redefinition of the second, or tests of fundamental constants that have not yet produced a deviation, into the wording. On the third, the two names are justified by origin and realisation of the concept, not by who holds a record number. Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and the Yb and Al+ groups reached comparable accuracy, and the citation should therefore avoid naming the record as the merit. Nothing said in round 1 changes my view of who the two names are.
statement.case_against: The overlap argument is legitimate and I have not dismissed it. A committee that sees the lattice clock as an application of the comb and of ion control would reasonably say precision timekeeping has been honoured twice already. Credit for the 10^-18 milestone is spread over several species and groups, and a two-name citation will leave out real contributors. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so part of the practical payoff is prospective. Finally, as Chair I moved to B029 after reading the opening ballots, so I should accept that my own preference was shaped by the committee's pattern of ranking. For that reason I have tried to test the case on its science and its attribution and not on the number of supporters.

responses.point: Kroll writes new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second into his B029 citation, while saying he does not argue from the redefinition.
responses.response: I accept that he does not rest the case on the redefinition, but I would still keep both phrases out of the citation. Nobody has used these clocks to find a violation of a constant, and the redefinition is a decision for metrology bodies, not a scientific result. A citation that points to them invites exactly the objection that the prize is paid for expectation. I would be content to say the clocks open new possibilities for tests, but not to name them as merit. On his Hall-laboratory disclosure, I think it should be recorded and treated as a disclosure, not a recusal. He claims no collaboration or shared funding with Katori or Ye, and the case is carried independently by Lindroth, Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson and me.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the citation should name the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, not a record number that several groups hold, and that the comb overlap with 2005 is smaller than the ballots suggest.
responses.response: I agree and I have changed my wording because of this. My round-1 citation put the 10^-18 level at the centre, and that is the part shared with Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and the ion-clock groups. The revised text names the invention and development of lattice clocks first, with the magic-wavelength trap in the formulation, and mentions 10^-18 only as the demonstrated outcome. Her point that the comb is the readout, not the source of accuracy, is the best short answer to the 2005 objection and I would use it in the committee's own rationale. Where I am less sure than she is is whether the 2012 overlap can be answered as quickly. I rely on the difference in trade-off between single-ion statistics and many-atom systematics, and I would want the rationale to state that difference in plain terms.

responses.point: Eriksson now regards his rank of B029 as too low and would support it, but says the clock rests on metrology that follows from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that DMFT introduces a more fundamental new idea.
responses.response: I welcome his willingness to support B029, and his candour about Metzner's omission in B035 is the reason I cannot move toward his own case. The conceptual weight of DMFT is real, but the attribution gap he names is a problem the three-name limit cannot fix. On his point about kind, I accept that the lattice clock is a different sort of contribution from a new theoretical framework. But I do not find that a reason against it. The magic-wavelength idea is a new principle in its own right, and it has been tested against independent clocks, which the committee can say about few other candidates. I would not call it a consequence of earlier prizes.

responses.point: Mehlig says independent confirmation of the performance is not independent confirmation of the credit, and wants the citation tied to the lattice-clock concept and not to comb or spectroscopy work honoured in 2005.
responses.response: That is a fair distinction and I accept it. Reproduction across laboratories shows the clock works, not that Katori and Ye are the right two names. The case for the names rests on origin and on first realisation: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme, and Ye's group turned it into the strontium clock that set the 10^-18 benchmark and revealed many-body effects. The committee should say that in the rationale and not lean on the confirmation list. I also agree with his reply to Lindroth that adding a second part would force a weaker partner and dilute the claim, so I am not proposing a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee finds that the lattice scheme is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, which the written rationale has to argue and not just assert.
Whether crediting only Katori and Ye is defensible against Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, which I cannot settle from the supplied record.
How much the pending redefinition of the second should affect the timing of the prize; I do not treat it as scientific evidence, but others may.
If B029 does not hold, whether B018 can resolve its overlap with 2012 and the NIST and Monroe credit, or B031 can settle the mechanism of its correlated states, before a prize is credible.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I have documented professional connections to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, and my KTH group works on gamma-ray polarimetry aimed at gamma-ray bursts, so I declare an interest in B013 and B037 and would stay out of any final decision on them. I have a CERN-trained experimental background that bears on B012. I have no specific conflict on B029, B018 or B031. I no longer list B013 as an alternative and I did not argue for it this round, partly for this reason and partly because the credit gap I raised myself (van Paradijs and the optical-identification teams) remains unresolved. I note Kroll's disclosure on B029 and treat it as a disclosure for the committee to weigh, not as a reason to exclude his view.
